It proceeds from himself, in full consciousness of free agency, toward the education that is to civilize him. Sarah's idea, Peabody writes, is an inheritance from her grandfather, a remarkable chief of the Piutes. A passage preserved in the copy recalls his story from Sarah's Life Among the Piutes.
57791-the-details-of-the-rocket-system:
The Details of the Rocket System is Colonel Congreve's official account of his war rockets, drawn up in 1814 and here reproduced from the original edition. The pamphlet shows the weapon's uses at sea and on land, with plates of the equipment.

Congreve's introduction explains the occasion.  He had declined command of the corps himself, content, he says, to have put the weapon into the regiment's hands. He points to its early laurels at Leipzig and on the Adour. Plates show the principal equipments and exercises, and cases of actual service are given as proof.
58037-the-pastime-of-pleasure-an-allegor:
Stephen Hawes wrote The Pastime of Pleasure, an allegorical poem, here reprinted for the Percy Society in 1845 from the edition of 1555. The society printed early English poetry, ballads, and popular literature from manuscripts and scarce books. This is the eighteenth volume of the set. Hawes was a groom of the chamber to Henry the Seventh.

His poem tells of Graunde Amoure, a knight led through the schools of the seven sciences by Dame Doctrine, toward La Belle Pucelle. It is a long dream-journey of love and learning, in rhyme royal stanzas. The Percy council list at the front is a roll of the age's antiquaries. Poetry fans get a Tudor allegory in a scholar's dress.
58101-ragged-homes-and-how-to-mend-them:
Bayly wrote Ragged Homes and How to Mend Them, a book on the homes of the London poor, printed in 1860 and already in its fifth thousand. She dedicated it, by permission, to the Earl of Shaftesbury, the great reformer. Her motto states her creed: the cornerstone of the commonwealth is the hearthstone.

Bayly calls her book a narrative of facts. She goes into the courts and alleys of places such as Kensington Potteries, whose oldest house is pictured, and shows how drink, filth, and despair wreck a home. Then she shows mending: visits, schools, savings, and faith. The book belongs to the first wave of Victorian writing that treated slum life as a problem with remedies.
58537-the-fall-of-jerusalem-a-poem:
Church the younger published this poem in three parts at London in 1823, printed by Weston of Crosby Row, Southwark, and priced at three shillings. The motto is Hosea's: they shall be wanderers among the nations. The dedication goes to the mistress of Brandeston Hall in Suffolk, whose kindness to his family the poet praises without flattery, he insists.

Ambition, he tells the reader, moves all men, some to name, some to state, some to a snug box a few miles from town. His education is too confined for publicity, his disposition too peaceful for politics, his imagination too boundless for trade. He writes to please his friends, at whose request the poem was made, and calls it his first and last essay. The fall of Jerusalem, in the verse of a Southwark amateur, is a young man's bid for a serious subject.
58556-the-lament-of-the-mormon-wife-a-po:
Marietta Holley's The Lament of the Mormon Wife, a poem with pictures, was published at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1880 by the American Publishing Company. The speaker is a wife grown old, and she opens on her own changed looks. The hair her husband once pressed from her girlish brow, brighter than the western light, has gone gray with the sunset.

She recalls the ring he set on her hand in a sheltered northern village, and his firm word that there would never be but one wife. Then a smooth-faced saint beguiled him with honeyed lies, and a shadow rose, small at first as her hand. The poem follows that shadow as it grows day by day over her marriage.
58692-the-vigil-of-brunhild-a-narrative-:
The Vigil of Brunhild, a narrative poem by Frederic Manning, was published by John Murray of London in 1907. Brunhild, queen of Austrasia and Burgundy, died in the year 613. Manning takes her as a figure of tragedy, betrayed by her own army and held by rebel nobles.

The poem shows her in her castle of Orbe, by the lake of Neuchâtel, in her last hours. She awaits the brutal death her captors hold in store. The poem is a chain of visions that come to her in that stress. Manning argues in his preface that narrative verse, smoother than drama, lets him show her whole complex soul at the moment of giving all up.
58749-inducements-to-the-colored-people-:
Inducements to the Colored People of the United States to Emigrate to British Guiana was printed at Boston in 1840. The pamphlet was compiled from statements and documents furnished by Edward Carbery, agent of the colony's Immigration Society and a proprietor there, and signed only A Friend to the Colored People.

Its first section sells the place. Guiana lies on the north-east coast of South America, between the mouths of the Orinoco and the Amazon. The British portion runs two hundred miles along the coast, from the Corentyn river, which divides it from Dutch Guiana, westward past the Morocco creek toward Venezuela. Inland it runs about two hundred miles to a mountain chain above Brazil. That is over forty thousand square miles, about the size of New York. Three great rivers, the Essequebo, the Demarara, and the Berbice, water it, and it never suffers the hurricanes of other tropics.
59036-the-york-problem:
Herbert D Kastle wrote the science fiction story The York Problem, which ran in Worlds of If magazine in February 1955. The story opens in a far future where thirteen men in the blue of their office sit round a table: the Earth Council of Prevention and Correction of Non-Conformity.

Commissioner Dobu reports that the juvenile delinquency problem in York has lasted some six hundred years, since the year 3046 by their reckoning. The people of York, ruled by church masters who call psychiatry a sacrilege, refuse all aid and schooling. The council coolly proposes the community's elimination, by sterilization or worse, as it has so often proposed before. A clerk named Mala Wang, bored by the routine report, carries the file onward. Kastle's tale is a cold satire on tidy councils and cruel solutions.
59377-powder-post-beetles-in-buildings-w:
Agriculture Department writers in Washington put out a short leaflet on beetles that eat wood from the inside. It is Leaflet 358 in the department series. The pests bore through beams, floors, and furniture, and leave fine powder in their tunnels. The grubs feed on starch and on the soft part of the wood.

The leaflet names the main kinds, from the southern lyctus beetle to the old house borer and the death-watch beetle. It tells how each kind looks and where it does harm. Control turns on the place and the scale of the attack. A spray may be enough for a small patch, while a bad case calls for fumigation. Home owners and builders get plain steps for saving wood.
60112-ireton-a-poem:
Ireton, published at London in 1827, is Thomas Bailey's poem on Henry Ireton, the republican general of the age of Charles the First. Bailey dedicated the poem to Lord John Russell and priced it at one shilling and sixpence. The idea came on a walk to Attenburrow, a village on the Trent near Nottingham, where Ireton was born.

In his preface Bailey says vice and folly, not kings alone, degrade a people. Morals, he argues, are the only sure base for civil liberty. He praises the reformers who sought plain habits of thought in politics and religion. The poem turns a Civil War hero into a lesson for a later age.
60397-as-time-glides-on-the-months-in-pi:
As Time Glides On is a gift book of the months in picture and poem, set in order by a named hand with prints by a team of artists. It was put out in London in a fine dress, with plates made by a noted print house of the day. A verse on the first page gives Time his own voice.

Time wears no purple of earth born kings, that verse says, and no white fur of lords. Yet king and court man, great as they be, must fall from their pomp and bend to him. His staff holds no gems, yet none can say they will not come under its sway. A chime and a dial tell who he is: Old King Time, lord of all the months that the book then takes in turn.
60957-the-court-of-chancery-a-satirical-:
Reginald James Blewitt, late of Lincoln's Inn, wrote The Court of Chancery, a satirical poem published at London in 1827. Lines from Byron front the poem: when knaves and fools combined over all prevail, when justice halts and right begins to fail. Blewitt inscribed the work to his father, Major Edward Blewitt of Llantarnam Abbey, with filial affection.

His preface opens with the charge: the great delay and ruinous expenses of a Chancery suit have become proverbial. In verse he attacks the court where suits outlived their suitors and costs ate estates whole. A young lawyer writing satire against his own profession took some nerve. Dickens's Bleak House would make the same charge famous a generation later. Blewitt's couplets are an early shot in a long war.
61259-the-telephone-in-america-bell-tele:
A Bell System booklet telling the story of the telephone in America. It begins in 1876, when Alexander Graham Bell first talked successfully over his primitive instrument, and comes down to a nation of more than fifty-four million telephones. About four-fifths of them belong to the Bell System, the group of local companies, research organization, and manufacturing company headed by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company.

The booklet stresses that Bell service is home town service: operators, installers, and managers are neighbors. Nine of every ten calls are local, yet the tenth may cross the continent or the ocean. Photographs show the new transcontinental microwave system, whose 107 relay stations first spanned the continent by air in 1951, carrying calls and television together.
61372-the-cruise-of-the-catalpa-a-poem:
The Cruise of the Catalpa is a tale poem by John Breslin, out at Boston in eighteen seventy-six. Breslin led the men who freed a band of Irish state felons from a jail in Australia. The poem was writ on board the ship of that deed. Its date is the Easter Monday of that year.

In rhyme with a gay lift the poem tells how six men slid off in a row past their guards. Names of the freed men roll past the verse as the jail men race and chase in vain. Teams haul the loads past sand hills to the shore. With guns in hand the men stand on white sand and push their boat off. A refrain asks what that is to any one, at the end of each verse, in a tone of blithe scorn.
61608-samantha-on-the-race-problem:
Marietta Holley wrote this dialect humor book, Samantha on the Race Problem, published at New York with copyright of 1892. She writes as Josiah Allen's Wife, the shrewd Samantha of the Jonesville tales, and pictures by Kemble fill the book. The contents list her characters: Uncle Nate Gowdey, Melinda, Deacon Henzy, Cleopatra, and the colored children. One picture caption reads: they wuz tracts and Bibles.

Samantha travels south and reports what she sees in her flat, commonsense voice. Holley used comedy to argue against lynching and for the humanity of Black southerners, inside jokes her huge readership would accept. The book is a period document twice over: earnest reform in dialect dress. Its pictures and chapter heads show both its courage and its time.
61726-through-afro-america-an-english-re:
Through Afro-America is a study of the race problem by William Archer. Chapman and Hall issued it in London in 1910. The book is dedicated to Wells, with a wry note. Archer so rarely disagreed with him that a book was needed. Part one is called Southward Ho. The black man's paradise and the South's nightmare open it. Louisville, Memphis, and New Orleans follow.

Two leaders, a white type and a black, are weighed. The black belt and a demonstration farm come next. Crime-slavery and debt-serfdom get hard chapters. Hampton and an industrial university are visited. Part three runs from Havana to Panama. Archer writes as an English critic abroad. His report is sharp, fair-minded, and unsparing.
63423-kathrina-a-poem:
Josiah Gilbert Holland, a beloved American editor and author, published his long poem Kathrina in 1867. This Scribner edition of 1893 lists his complete works in sixteen volumes, from Bitter-Sweet to Sevenoaks. Holland dedicated the poem to Elizabeth, the wife of his heart, as the page says.

Kathrina follows a woman's life in three parts: childhood and youth, love, and labor. A tribute and smaller poems stand between the parts. Holland wrote for the hearth, and his plain, earnest verse sold hugely in postwar America. Kathrina was a parlor favorite, read aloud in families who trusted Holland's counsel on work, faith, and home as much as his poetry.
6442-bitter-sweet-a-poem:
J. G. Holland builds Bitter Sweet as a poem in movements, each stating and illustrating one question. A prelude and first movement state and argue the question in talk. A first episode illustrates it by nature, and a second movement tells it by experience. A second episode illustrates it by story, a third movement works it out in drama, and an envoy closes. The picture opens on winter's wild birthnight, wind moaning in the fretful east.

Sleet sifts onto huddled leaves and pins them to earth, while a roofless bullock hugs a sheltering stack with dumb endurance. A mid passage turns darker and stranger: the milk haired heifer's life must pass to fill our own, as grass passed to feed her. From lowly woe springs lordly joy, Holland writes, and life's cup passes hand to hand up being's gradation. The poem argues that loss feeds life.
64891-a-pair-of-them:
Pair of Them is a story for young readers by Evelyn Raymond. Crowell published it in New York with rights held in 1901. A Sunshine Library list of tales for children fronts the volume. Aunt Hannah and Seth, The Blind Brother, and The Captain's Dog stand there. Chapter one, Where the Houses are Big, opens the tale itself.

Bonny-Gay, a little girl, talks with the Gray Gentleman by a monument. He asks how she came by her queer name as they sit. She was born on a Sunday morning, she tells him with a smile. Her big black dog Max stays close as she hugs him tight. Where the houses are small and how the pair met follow in turn.
65495-what-cheer-or-roger-williams-in-ba:
Job Durfee wrote What Cheer, a poem on Roger Williams in banishment, revised and edited by Thomas Durfee for an edition printed at Providence in 1896. The title takes the greeting, What Cheer, that tradition ties to Williams's meeting with the Narragansett people. An epigraph quotes Williams's own letter on fourteen weeks tossed between friends in a bitter cold winter.

The editor's notice owns that he cut some stanzas and altered others. He says the changes only clear the sense and ease the verse, never the meaning. Notes and an appendix follow the poem, with a few shorter pieces added. The poem tells how Williams, cast out of Massachusetts Bay for his views on conscience, founded Providence. It is Rhode Island's tribute to its founder, in verse.
66140-test-problem:
Alan J Ramm wrote Test Problem, a short science fiction tale in Imagination in November nineteen hundred fifty three. Jeremy Hovah walks to room 16B for his last exam. Six years at the university hang on this one course. Its name is Advanced Deliberation and Memory.

Jeremy cut classes and knows his odds look poor. He slips his record card in a slot and sits at the dials. A calm voice gives his task from a hid speaker. He must rebuild a star system in a far space sector. Only raw stuff of space and his trained mind may be used. Life forms must match the model too. Ten minutes of prints flood his mind, and then his hands fly.
66174-the-english-prison-system:
The English Prison System is a state tale of the jails of England and Wales by their own chief. He was a knight who chaired the board for those jails and led the world guild of that craft. It came out in the first years past the great war, from houses round the world.

Its parts take the sense of jail reform first, then the board itself and its rules of fault and pain. The tale of hard time in gangs comes next, with its form in the day of print. Held back time for the worst, plain jail, and the great ask of a past age lead to the laws of the age. Youth and its woes close the span.
66946-summer-morning-a-poem:
Thomas Miller, the basket-maker poet of London, wrote this poem, published in 1841. His earlier books crowd the title page: Rural Sketches, Beauties of the Country, Fair Rosamond, and Gideon Giles. Miller rose from the workbench to the booksellers' lists by his pen.

The poem opens as morning breaks through the mines of heaven and shakes her jeweled skirts on the sky. Vassal clouds bow and catch her scattered gems of pearl and ruby. No sheep-track has yet crushed a flower, and the spider's web hangs silvered with dew. Readers get a working man's dawn, in the full romantic manner of his day.
67365-a-personal-problem:
Bedford-Jones wrote this tale of the South Seas trading world. It opens at a commissioner's house on an island, where all the island is gathered for the night. Steamer day has brought a bale of ice up from Auckland, a true luxury in the tropics.

A fat man named Hobson faces an old enemy across the table. The lean man, Cranshaw, reveals that he is also John Smith, the firm's agent at Raratonga, a fact Hobson never guessed. Hobson had driven him out of Auckland, taken his stock, and married Agnes into the bargain. Now the reckoning comes, with icy politeness. Readers get a sharp tale of revenge served cold in the islands.
67683-the-boys-book-of-model-aeroplanes-:
Francis A Collins wrote The Boys’ Book of Model Aeroplanes, a guide to build and fly small craft. Eveleigh Nash issued the book in London in nineteen hundred twelve. Collins took the photos and drew the charts himself. He gave the book to his son Arnold, age ten, his keen help.

Part one calls model flight the new sport for boys. Why a wing lifts gets a clear first lesson. A glider build comes next, then a motor of wound strands. Fine points of craft fill a full chapter of hints. Single wing and twin wing forms each get plans. Faults and their cures close the bench part. Part two tells how full flight grew, with the Wright brothers’ own tale in the midst.
67997-the-prodigal-pro-tem:
Frederick Orin Bartlett wrote this novel of the road, printed by Small, Maynard at Boston with a copyright of 1910. Christy drew the pictures. Barnes, its hero, stands in a summer valley at the start and finds the picture lacks one thing: a young and very fair woman.

Three fingered Bill, questions of diplomacy, and the call of the road carry Barnes outward. Chapters weigh what makes a prodigal. John gives his notice; an old prodigal comes home; a young prodigal comes home after him. Barnes learns a great truth, and so does his mother. Aunt Philomela gambles near the end, and everyone learns something in the last chapter. Bartlett writes sunny romance, where the road complicates matters and then untangles them. The title means a prodigal for the time being.
68041-the-west-point-rivals-or-mark-mall:
Lieutenant Frederick Garrison wrote The West Point Rivals, or Mark Mallory's Stratagem, dated nineteen hundred and three. Street and Smith issued the tale in the Boys' Own Library at seventy-five cents. Garrison had written other West Point tales.

Mark Mallory is the hero cadet, and Bull Harris is his foe. Chapters bring a circus at Highland Falls, fun with the yearlings, and mortar practice. A front picture shows a man calmly writing down the names of cadets he sees. A desperate plot, a camp in the woods, and a trap for Mallory follow. Mallory is caught in the trap before the end of it all. School pride and pluck rule.
68386-book-of-parlor-tricks-how-to-perfo:
Book of Parlor Tricks, a small how-to booklet, came out at Boston in April 1895. It formed number sixteen, volume two, of the Multum in Parvo Library. The series called itself the smallest magazine in the world. Single copies cost five cents. The first trick, the Diviner, rests on a private pact between two players. The chosen word follows an item with four legs in a spoken list.

Other tricks include walking on a hot iron bar and restoring a burnt ribbon. The ribbon trick uses a twin piece hid in the palm. A problem shows how to soften an egg in vinegar and slip it into a bottle. The tricks use cheap props and patter suited to home shows.
68614-historic-doorways-of-old-salem:
Mary Harrod Northend wrote and photographed this guide to the fine old doorways of Salem, Massachusetts, published in 1926 by Houghton Mifflin. The catalog title is cut short; the title page gives the full name as Historic Doorways of Old Salem. Northend argues that a doorway shows the character of a house and of the people who built it.

After short chapters on how the Salem doorway changed over time, the book walks house by house. The Rebecca Nurse house, the John Ward house, the Pickering house, and dozens more each get a short account with a photograph. Many of the houses date from the colonial and early sea trade years. The book serves readers who love old houses and New England history.
69186-the-narcotic-drug-problem:
The Narcotic Drug Problem is a medical study of addiction by Ernest S. Bishop, published by the Macmillan Company of New York in 1920. Bishop was clinical professor of medicine at the New York Polyclinic Medical School. He had served as resident physician for the alcoholic, narcotic, and prison service at Bellevue Hospital.

Bishop also sat on the narcotic committee of the Conference of Judges and Justices of New York State. His committee work on habit-forming drugs joined medicine to law at the moment of strict new drug controls. The book speaks from hospital and courtroom experience rather than from theory alone. It is dedicated to his wife. As a document of how American medicine framed addiction in 1920, it shows a doctor arguing inside a system turning toward punishment.
69841-the-boy-s-book-of-trades-and-the-t:
The Boy's Book of Trades and the Tools Used in Them is a guide by one of the authors of England's Workshops, issued at London in 1866. Its contents list some thirty trades, from brickmaker to gun maker. A preface opens with the dignity of work.

Happiness depends mainly on the work a man does and how he does it, the preface argues. Idleness is ignorance or wickedness, it scolds. Mason, carpenter, plumber, and blacksmith each get a chapter of tools and ways. Cabinet maker, calico printer, tanner, and hatter fill the long list. Readers get a Victorian lad's tour of the workshops that built his world.
69859-table-traits-with-something-on-the:
Doran's Table Traits, with Something on Them was published in London in 1854 by Richard Bentley, with Oliver & Boyd in Edinburgh and Hodges & Smith in Dublin. It was sold at the railway stations too. Doran inscribes the volume to Henry, Earl of Harewood, in grateful memory of bygone happy years. A French tag from Brillat Savarin heads the title page.

The contents are styled a bill of fare, and a long one. The legend of Amphitryon serves as prologue, then diet and digestion, water, and breakfast with its materials: corn, bread, tea, coffee, chocolate. The old coffee houses and the French cafes follow, the ancient cook and the modern, and a sketch of Careme. Dinner traits, sauces, the parasite, wine and its making, the Caesars at table, English kings at theirs, strange banquets, and supper wind the feast up.
70010-the-shadow-between-them:
McVeigh Miller wrote this love story, issued in the New Eagle Series as number 1078 at fifteen cents. The series called its books popular copyrights and carefully selected love stories. Its list is full of tales by Georgie Sheldon, Charles Garvice, Harriet Lewis, and May Agnes Fleming, all running to some three hundred pages. Miller's name stands in that company, and this novel is offered in the same line.

The title promises a shadow between two lovers, the stuff of the dime novel romance. Such books sold by the hundred thousand to readers who wanted strong feeling, secrets, and a hard-won happy ending. The publisher's note boasts that every title stays always in print. The volume is a fair sample of cheap American romance fiction of its day.
70326-the-art-of-preserving-health-a-poe:
The Art of Preserving Health is a long poem on how to keep the body sound. A Millar sold the book in the Strand in London in seventeen hundred forty four. Sewed copies cost four shillings. Book one, on air, opens the song with a call to a goddess.

Hygeia, queen of joy, is asked to come down and teach. Her smile, the poet says, holds back pain and plague. Foul air from swamps, fields of war, and rot all flee her light. Sharp shifts from cold to hot breed ills in her realm. The poet owns his task is hard in verse. Dry rules of health must sing and stay clear at once. Old lore on Nile fevers guides his steps as he starts.
70537-the-city-of-jerusalem:
The City of Jerusalem, by Colonel C R Conder, was printed in London by John Murray in 1909. Conder had written Tent Work in Palestine, Heth and Moab, Syrian Stone Lore, and The Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem. A model of Herod Temple by Miss M A Duthoit stands at the front.

Chapters open with an opening survey, then the city before David and under the Hebrew kings. Ezra and Nehemiah, the Greek age, and Herod the Great follow. The Gospel sites and the fall of Jerusalem fill the mid part. The Roman city, the Byzantines, the Arabs, and the Turks come in turn. The Latin kingdom and Franks and Moslems close the tale. Conder first saw the city one summer morning in 1872, a mile off, with its long grey wall. Bible land fans get a soldier scholar city history.
70834-the-negro-the-southerner-s-problem:
The Negro: The Southerner's Problem is a volume of essays by Thomas Nelson Page. Scribner's published it in New York in 1904. Page dedicates the studies to all who truly wish to help solve the race problem. His introduction makes no claim to have fully discussed the subject. Years of study and familiarity with some phases of it stand behind the attempt. He promises to present them plainly, candidly, and temperately.

Page admits that no man can wholly free himself from his upbringing. His propositions may rest on imperfect information, he concedes. Still, he says, none was advanced without what he took for sound authority. The essays treat the race question as it stood in the South of his day. He notes that hopes of settlement had often brightened, then been dashed. The question kept returning in new and menacing forms.
71246-swiss-allmends-and-a-walk-to-see-t:
Swiss Allmends and a Walk to See Them describes the common lands of Switzerland. Zincke wrote the travel study. Smith, Elder published it in London in 1874. Zincke was vicar of Wherstead and a royal chaplain. The book forms a second month in Switzerland. A good map of the whole country is prefixed.

A preface explains the study's origin. His first month's sketch had omitted the allmends. Those commonable lands deserved attention of their own. Swiss officials and scholars helped his inquiry. The excursion itself covered more varied ground than the first. A chapter on Einsiedeln treats the religion of the region. Understanding a people, he argues, includes understanding their faith. The narrative of the walk runs unbroken by digressions.
7184-a-heart-song-of-to-day-disturbed-by:
Annie G. Savigny's novel opens with a pretty woman laying a plot and hiring a gardener, and its chapter titles keep that game of masks and motives going. Madame shuffles the cards, Vaura moves through a medley, and Lionel Trevalyon enters a story of love and love-making where velvet paws hide claws. Society bouquets, fates spinning black thread, and flights from earth to earth mark the turns.

Savigny writes a society tale in which talk, scheme, and feeling pull against each other, and the heroine's heart-song is disturbed by the unruly member of the title. The long chapter list promises intrigue, romance, and sharp social comedy in equal share. Readers follow a world where a glance can be a move in a larger game.
72180-requiem:
Edmond Hamilton wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Amazing Stories in April 1962, drawn by Summers. Its head note asks whether even Earth's death must be stripped of dignity by mass media chatter. Captain Kellon thinks sourly that he commands not a starship but a travelling circus. Telaudio men, commentators, and publicity seekers crowd his ship.

His crew once pushed knowledge ever further into the galaxy for the Survey. Now they carry costly passengers on a sentimental mission. Ahead shines a white dwarf sun, cold for two thousand years. Its planets have lain frozen and ice locked all that time. Kellon orders the ship in, hating the errand.
72831-left-over-foods-and-how-to-use-the:
Left-Over Foods and How to Use Them is a home book by Elizabeth Hiller, writ for a cold box firm of a mid state. It came out with rights in nineteen ten. Its full name adds hints on the keep of foods in the home. A plate heads the book. Hiller opens past a quote she will not grant, that scraps are mere chance bits fit for no cost or work.

The left bits of a plain house are worth care, she holds, and past small work and cost turn to the most sweet foods. The loose toss of left foods past a foul name is what bred the hate of made up plates, she says. Hash it self is a much wronged word and mix. A part on how to weigh and mix with care is bid as the first study of the book.
73759-the-ships-and-sailors-of-old-salem:
Ralph Paine wrote this history of Salem's shipping, copyrighted in 1908 and issued in a new edition at Chicago in 1912. The catalog title is a scrap of its subtitle, the record of a brilliant era of American achievement. A photo shows the Panay, one of the last Salem ships, bound from Boston to Manila. The first chapter calls Salem a port of vanished fleets.

Chapters follow Philip English and his era, early pirates, and the privateersmen of 1776. Captain Jonathan Haraden and Captain Luther Little get their own tales, and a sailor's journal of the Revolution is printed. Paine quotes Kipling and an old chantey at his start. His book recalls the days when Salem's merchantmen sailed where none had sailed.
73783-books-and-how-to-make-the-most-of-:
Books and How to Make the Most of Them is a guide by James Hosmer Penniman. Bardeen of Syracuse issued the book in nineteen eleven for school readers. Penniman opens that advice on reading is both common and much needed. Even Goethe said he had spent fifty years learning how to read.

Chapter one calls a book a miracle wrought by human agency in print. Black lines on a white page can carry a life thought in a pocket. A book beats the telegraph, Penniman says, for it kills time as well. Later chapters treat how to use books and how to train memory. What to read, the art of reading, and kinds of books follow.
73820-batiks-and-how-to-make-them:
Batiks, and How to Make Them is a craft manual by Pieter Mijer, published by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1921. The first edition was printed in 1919, and three more followed within two years. Photographs by Harting fill the book, starting with a Chinese screen panel by Mijer and Emile Weeckers.

The chapters open with batik in Java, where the art has flourished since old times, and batik in Holland. Then come tools and materials, the tjanting wax pen, and the batik process itself. Sound dyeing and the value of a dye record close the teaching. Pictures show native sarongs, fish designs, and batik used in home decoration.
73866-the-motherless-bairns-and-who-shel:
Motherless Bairns, and Who Sheltered Them, is a tale for the young from the Religious Tract Society. The society published it in London from Paternoster Row and Saint Paul Churchyard. Contents list seven chapters for the story of the little orphans of its plate. Motherless and Homeless opens the book at page five of the volume.

The Door on the Latch, The Ragged School, and Bessie and Her Teacher follow in the list. Seaside Pleasures, The Harbour of Refuge, and Found After Many Days close the contents shown. It opens on a sharp, frosty night late in December, with snow driving in gusts at the corner of a street. The tale is a waif story of the tract kind, in which shelter, school, and seaside charity remake the lives of two children. Such small books were given by the million in Sunday schools of the Victorian age.
73870-negro-life-in-new-york-s-harlem:
Wallace Thurman wrote Negro Life in New York's Harlem for the Little Blue Book series, number 494. E Haldeman-Julius edited the series, and his company printed the booklet in Girard, Kansas. The subtitle promises a lively picture of a popular and interesting section. Thurman opens by listing Harlem's many nicknames.

Harlem, he writes, has been called the Mecca of the New Negro and the capital of Black America. One chapter counts two hundred thousand Black residents. Others treat social life, night life, and amusements in turn. House rent parties, the numbers game, church life, and Black journalism each get a chapter. The booklet closes by naming Harlem the Mecca of the New Negro. It is a quick, vivid survey from inside the Renaissance.
74463-slavery-as-an-industrial-system:
Nieboer wrote a study of slavery as a work system, in a second revised edition issued at the Hague in 1910. The first edition came out in 1900. Nieboer confines his facts to the life of peoples he calls savage tribes, and he builds his case by close comparison.

The part on where slavery is found grew much in this edition, as fresh facts came in. Nieboer thanks his teacher Steinmetz of Amsterdam for help on both editions. He hopes the work aids more than the tale of old life: he wants laws that help explain how all human groups are built and how work is shared.
74783-boynton-bicycle-railway-system:
Boynton Bicycle Railway System is a promotional pamphlet of 1896 for a one-rail railway. Its company kept an office at 32 Nassau Street in New York, with Eben Moody Boynton as president. A picture shows a bicycle electric car in use at Bellport, Long Island. The car had run 7,500 miles and reached sixty miles an hour.

The pamphlet argues from the bicycle itself, which carries ten times its own weight. Its cars stand two stories tall, about four feet wide and fourteen feet deep, built of veneer and steel. The aim is to cut friction and sway. Lighter cars would run faster and safer, and wear rails and stock far less.
75024-our-presidents-and-how-we-make-the:
Our Presidents and How We Make Them, by McClure, is a history of American presidential elections issued by Harper in 1900. A portrait of the author fronts the illustrated book. The contents open with the Washington elections of 1789 to 1792. The Adams and Jefferson contest of 1796 follows in its turn.

Contest by contest, the book marches down the century of elections. The Jefferson, Adams, and Burr fight of 1800 gets its chapter. Madison, Monroe, and the great four way contest of 1824 follow. Jackson and his rivals fill the next long stretch of the table. McClure was a party manager and editor who knew the game himself. He tells how conventions, bargains, and crowds make a president.
75563-cedar-chests-how-to-make-them:
Ralph Windoes wrote Cedar Chests: How to Make Them, a shop manual from the Bruce Publishing Company of Milwaukee. The catalog title is only the copyright line, and the catalog names the publisher as creator. Windoes had taught manual training at a high school in Davenport, Iowa. This enlarged second edition carries copyrights of 1918 and 1921.

The chapters start with the wood itself, the red cedar whose scent guards woolens from moths. Windoes then shows how to build a simple chest, step by step. Long sections give designs, the finishing of cedar, and copper trimmings. A last chapter covers matting boxes. One picture shows a chest said to have come over on the Mayflower. The book served school shops and home woodworkers who wanted a sound, sweet smelling chest of their own making.
76302-french-morality-under-the-regulati:
French Morality under the Regulation System is an English version of chapters from Julie Daubié's book on the poor woman in the nineteenth century, printed in London and Liverpool in 1870. Daubié's work came from many years of research and self-denying labor among the poor and the outcasts of society. Her permission letter is dated from Paris in January 1870.

The chapters bear on the most unhappy of her countrywomen: the registered prostitutes of France under the regulation system. Daubié calls instead for laws to punish seduction, wages that make women independent, and a ban on provocations in the public way. The English edition carried her case to the repeal campaign then gathering force.
77390-a-child-shall-lead-them:
Mary E Ropes wrote these tales for the Sunday School Union of London. The volume holds three pieces: A Child Shall Lead Them, The House That Jack Built, and Another Moses. The first tale takes its shape from the old cumulative rhyme, retold here as a story with a moral.

The House That Jack Built here is a grand public-house at a London street corner, kept by John Drinkrow. Its plate glass, bright lights, and warm welcome lure wayfarers like a marsh light, Ropes warns, to ruin. The tale turns a child's rhyme into a temperance story about drink and the home. Pictures show scenes such as Ratcliffe the prodigal.
77753-the-population-problem:
Alexander Carr-Saunders, a biologist and social scientist, published The Population Problem at Oxford in 1922. Its subtitle calls the book a study in human evolution. Carr-Saunders sorted population questions into two kinds, numbers and quality.

He traces talk about numbers from Greece and Rome to the modern age. For centuries, he notes, dense populations seemed a clear good. Then writers began to weigh mouths against food, and Malthus published his famous book in 1798. Carr-Saunders reviews that history to frame his own study. The book became a standard text in early population studies, read by biologists and reformers alike.
7804-expressive-voice-culture-including-:
Jessie Eldridge Southwick, teacher at Emerson College of Oratory, sets out the Emerson system in Expressive Voice Culture. The system treats voice as a natural reporter of the person, always tending to express a thought or feeling in fitting tone. The book links technique to expression throughout.

Southwick warns she offers one person's contribution, not a full science. Yet her first chapter grounds voice work in meaning: the ring of true culture lies in perfect modulation of tone and movement. Speakers, teachers, and readers aloud will find plain methods for making voice match thought.
78562-an-englishwoman-in-a-turkish-harem:
An Englishwoman in a Turkish Harem is a set of letters by Grace Ellison, first published in London in 1915. Methuen and Company issued the book from Essex Street with thirteen illustrations. Browne of Cambridge wrote its introduction for this edition. Ellison is shown in Turkish costume in the frontispiece photograph of the volume.

She dedicates the letters to all who made her visit so interesting and happy, and most of all to her friend and hostess. Her earlier books include Abdul Hamid Daughter, written with Melek Hanoum, and A Turkish Woman European Impressions, written with Zeyneb Hanoum. Those partnerships frame this book, which reports life inside a harem from a guest place within it. Few English books of the war years could claim that vantage. The letters let an Englishwoman describe Ottoman domestic life at first hand, in the last years before that world ended.
8146-victor-roy-a-masonic-poem:
Harriett Annie Wilkins wrote Victor Roy as a Masonic poem, dedicated by permission to Daniel Spry, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Canada. Her preface explains that an anecdote in The Craftsman gave rise to the poem, and that it aims neither at Alpine heights of imagination nor at undiscovered treasures of thought. It is a very simple story, told in very simple words, about lives like those around us, sorrows daily borne, and faith that gives strength to suffering humanity.

The poem's Masonic character lies in its moral: brotherhood, endurance, and trust in dark times. Wilkins writes plainly, for readers rather than critics, and her verses suit reading aloud in a lodge or at home. As Canadian verse of its period, it preserves a modest, sincere voice, and a glimpse of Masonic ideals in poetry.
8536-philip-gilbert-hamerton-an-autobiog:
Philip Gilbert Hamerton tells his own life from 1834 to 1858 in this autobiography, and his wife continues it as a memoir from 1858 to 1894. Hamerton opens on intellectual living. It is not so much an accomplishment as a state of mind, seeking earnestly for the highest and purest truth, even while blundering for want of perfect wisdom and clear light.

Hamerton, an art critic and writer on French life, lived between England and France, and the double narrative follows his formation and his career. Readers get a Victorian life in art and letters, told first by the man himself, then by the woman who knew him best. The volume suits readers of art criticism and of Victorian biography.
8683-the-columbiad-a-poem:
Joel Barlow published The Columbiad in 1809 as an epic poem on Columbus and the founding of America, prefaced by careful remarks on his design. Barlow admits the difficulty of fitting so vast and recent a subject to classical epic form, and of making it both poetical and persuasive. An Italian epigraph from Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered sets Columbus beside Hercules and Bacchus, as a hero whose fame will outlast empires.

The poem follows Columbus's voyage and, in prophetic vision, the rise of the American republic, its institutions, and its future glory. Barlow, diplomat and poet, wrote as a convinced republican, and the epic doubles as political argument in verse. Modern readers may find its optimism and its rhetoric dated, but it remains the most ambitious American epic of its generation, and a key text for the early republic's self-image.
9047-the-banks-of-wye-a-poem:
Robert Bloomfield wrote this poem in four books after a summer trip down the River Wye in 1807 with friends from Gloucestershire. The poem, printed in 1811, follows the party through South Wales, noting river scenes, hills, and the people met on the way. Bloomfield dedicates it to the friends who shared the jaunt.

The verse is gentle and observant, praising the Wye's beauty in plain, musical lines rather than grand rhetoric. It belongs to the age of the picturesque tour, when travelers sought wild scenery with a sketchbook in hand. Modern readers can still enjoy it as a leisurely river journey in verse.
9092-the-farmer-s-boy-a-rural-poem:
Robert Bloomfield's rural poem made him famous, and this third edition shows its early success. The Farmer's Boy follows a shepherd's boy through the seasons, at work with flocks, fields, and country folk. Bloomfield, a working man, wrote from life, not from books. A sonnet by a young lady friend fronts the volume.

The poem praises honest labor, the turn of the year, and the quiet pride of farm life. Its plain verse won readers who seldom read poetry at all. Bloomfield's boy remains a touching figure, and the poem a landmark of English pastoral verse.
9985-pocahontas-a-poem:
Virginia Carter Castleman's narrative poem tells the story of Pocahontas in eight parts, opening with the little princess of her people. Castleman dedicates the poem to Virginia, the mother state, laying one leaf upon its wreath of fame.

The poem follows Pocahontas from childhood among her people through her meeting with the English settlers and the choices that made her famous in two worlds. Castleman writes in a descriptive, patriotic manner suited to school and home reading. Readers get the familiar legend retold as verse, with sympathy for its heroine.
a-heart-song-of-to-day-disturbed-by-fire:
Mrs. Annie G. Savigny signed A Heart-Song of To-Day as a society novel, and its chapter titles promise plots laid by pretty women, cards shuffled by a Madame, and hearts stirred in drawing rooms. The story moves among Vaura, Lionel Trevalyon, and their fashionable circle, where calls, balls, and confidences carry the action forward.

Madame works her schemes through gardeners, letters, and careful talk, while younger characters fall in and out of love under her eye. Chapters lift veils, take the season's mood on the wing, and return to earth with proposals and reversals. The result is a period piece of manners and intrigue, written for readers who liked their romance dressed in satin and spite.
anthem:
Ayn Rand's novella opens with a confession: it is a sin, the narrator says, to write words no others are meant to see. He lives in a future city where men speak of themselves only as 'we,' and the Council of Vocations assigns every person his life's work. Alone in a tunnel by candlelight, he writes his secret journal.

Twelve short parts trace his forbidden experiments with a strange power he finds in a forgotten tunnel, his love for a woman he names to himself, and his flight beyond the city. In the wild he finds an old house and its books. There he recovers a word his world had banned: I.
bitter-sweet-a-poem:
Bitter-Sweet, a poem by J G Holland, is a philosophical poem built like a symphony. Holland's contents divide it into movements. A prelude and a first movement, marked colloquial, state and argue the question. Episodes illustrate it by nature and by story. A second movement is narrative, a third dramatic. The denouement and an envoy close the design. Persons are listed like a cast.

The poem opens on winter's wild birthnight, with wind sighing through mountain gorges and pines. Holland, a bestselling poet and editor, asks why life mixes its gifts with pain. The question is argued, sung, and storied in turn. Bitter-Sweet was among the most read American poems of its century. Families kept it beside the Bible and read the movements aloud. Its symphony structure was the ambition of the age: to make a poem carry what an orchestra carries, argument included.
britannica-1911-archean-system:
Archean system is a geological term for the oldest rocks. The name derives from a Greek word for beginning. These rocks lie below the lowest fossil-bearing strata. Cambrian rocks with Olenellus fauna mark that boundary. A great mass of ancient rock sits beneath them. Stratified, metamorphic, and igneous rocks compose it. Pre-Cambrian is the general term for the whole assemblage. Subdivision is possible in many large tracts.

The Archean proper is the lowermost group. Granitoid, gneissic, and schistose characters prevail there. Its origin is mainly igneous. Sedimentary-looking groups lie above it in sequence. A special name helps where distinction is clear. The long article surveys regions worldwide. Old World and New World examples both appear. Terminology disputes receive careful attention. Geikie's Text Book of Geology anchors references. Chamberlin and Salisbury's Geology also features. John Allen Howe signs the survey.
britannica-1911-arnhem:
Arnhem is the capital of the province of Gelderland in Holland, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica paints the town and its setting. It stands on the right bank of the Rhine, about thirty-five miles by rail east of Utrecht. Its people numbered 57,240 in 1900.

The entry calls it a gay, fashionable town at the foot of the Veluwe hills, prized for its wooded, hilly country, which drew many rich families near. It picks out the great church of Saint Eusebius, with the marble monument to Charles, last duke of Gelderland, and its tower with a chime of forty-five bells. The town hall, built as a palace, bears the nickname devil's house for its odd carving.
britannica-1911-baldwin-i-king-of-jerusa:
Baldwin I was prince of Edessa from 1098 to 1100 and then the first king of Jerusalem, reigning to 1118. A brother of Godfrey of Bouillon, he had begun life as a clerk in orders. In 1096 he joined the First Crusade and marched with his brother into Asia Minor.

At Edessa he came first as protector, then, after Thoros was killed, as ruler. Called to Jerusalem on Godfrey's death, he was crowned king on Christmas Day 1100. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his wars in detail. Coast towns such as Arsuf, Caesarea, Acre, Beirut, and Sidon fell to him. Attacks from Egypt were beaten back, and his rule reached toward the Red Sea.
britannica-1911-baldwin-ii-king-of-jerus:
Baldwin II, first known as Baldwin de Burg, was count of Edessa from 1100 to 1118 and then king of Jerusalem until 1131. A son of Count Hugh of Rethel, he was a nephew of Godfrey of Bouillon and of Baldwin I, and he marched with Godfrey on the First Crusade.

Left in charge of Edessa when his cousin took the crown, he raided his Muslim neighbours for years. In 1104 he was beaten and captured, and Tancred held Edessa during his captivity. Freed early in 1108, he had to fight Tancred to regain his county. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his stern, successful rule at that far northern outpost.
britannica-1911-barents-willem:
Willem Barents (died 1597) was a Dutch navigator, born about the middle of the 16th century. In 1594 he left Amsterdam with two ships to seek a north-east passage to eastern Asia. He reached the west coast of Novaya Zemlya and followed it north until ice forced him back near its northern tip.

A second voyage in 1595, with seven ships, came too late to find open water. On the third, his ship was beset after rounding the north of Novaya Zemlya, and the crew wintered in the ice. The party escaped in open boats in June 1597, but Barents died on 30 June. The 1911 Britannica entry notes the later finding of his winter house and relics in 1871, and of part of his journal in 1875.
britannica-1911-bilderdijk-willem:
Willem Bilderdijk (1756–1831) was a Dutch poet, son of an Amsterdam physician. An accident to his foot at age six kept him from active life for ten years. In that idleness he formed habits of hard, close study. His parents backed the House of Orange with ardour. Bilderdijk grew up with strong monarchist and Calvinist views. Da Costa called him anti-revolutionary and anti-liberal on every front he listed.

He took a law doctorate at Leiden in 1782 and practised at The Hague. In 1795 he refused the oath to the new regime and had to leave Holland. Years in Hamburg, London, and Braunschweig followed in exile. The 1911 Britannica entry lists volume after volume of his poems, many written with his second wife. His collected poetical works filled sixteen volumes in the Haarlem edition. His letters and life records fill several more.
britannica-1911-binary-system:
Binary system, in astronomy, names a pair of two stars that revolve around each other. Their mutual attraction, or gravity, holds the pair together on that shared path. The 1911 Britannica entry is a short note of a few lines. It records a change in how astronomers classed such pairs. A line was once drawn between double stars seen to revolve and pairs with no observed motion. That line has been given up since, the entry explains.

The reason is a new general view of double stars. Astronomers now hold that all double stars must really be binary systems. Pairs that show no motion are taken as binaries whose movement has not yet been caught. The entry gives no example stars, periods, or discoverers in its brief space. It sends the reader elsewhere for the working detail of orbits. Its point is the change of definition itself, stated plainly and briefly.
britannica-1911-boarding-out-system:
Boarding out, in English poor law, means placing orphan or left children with fit foster parents. A 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry sets out how the system worked. It was first allowed in eighteen sixty eight. Some boards had in fact done it on their own for years before.

Two orders from eighteen eighty nine govern the practice. One covers placements inside a union, the other those outside it. The sum paid to foster parents was capped at a weekly rate per child. Critics said few working men could raise their own children for so little. That meant boarded children might be better off than their peers. Backers said the children got a natural home life and merged with ease into the wider world.
britannica-1911-brummagem:
Brummagem is an old local form of the name Birmingham, and the word carries a sneer. It was first applied to a counterfeit coin made in Birmingham, England, in the 17th century, and later to the plated and imitation articles made there. From coins and cheap metal goods the sense widened until it meant anything cheap, showy or tawdry.

Politics borrowed the insult too. Supporters of the Exclusion Bill in 1680 were particularly called Brummagems, with the meaning of sham Protestants. Their Tory opponents against the Bill were in turn nicknamed Anti-Birminghams or Brummagems, so both sides of that fight wore the label. The short entry holds the word's path from a city's name, through false coin and plated ware, to a standing term for shoddy show and sham religion.
britannica-1911-carboniferous-system:
The Carboniferous system is a great series of rocks in geology. It lies above the Devonian and below the Permian. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the system. Its strata include volcanic rocks as well as layered ones. W. D. Conybeare first applied the name in 1821. He used it for the coal-bearing strata of England and Wales. The grits and limestones beneath them were included.

The name rests on the coal seams in the system. Yet coal forms only a small part of its total thickness. The rocks include marine limestones, shales and sandstones. Fresh-water and estuarine beds also occur in the series. Oil-bearing rocks, gypsum and salt appear among them. The article notes the system's blurred edges in many lands. Its rocks merge into the Devonian below without a sharp line. Its fossils likewise merge into the Permian above.
britannica-1911-cochem:
Cochem is a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province on the Mosel, 30 miles west of Coblenz by the railway to Trier. Its people number 3,500 in the entry's count. Above the town the railway enters the longest tunnel in Germany, at two and a half miles. That tunnel and the river valley together fix the town's setting in the account given here.

Romantic situation is the town's chief quality as described, in the deep and winding valley of the Mosel. It sits at the foot of a hill surrounded by a feudal castle dating from 1051. That castle has been restored in its former style, the entry notes in its brief history. A considerable trade in wines is carried on at Cochem, the one industry named for the town.
britannica-1911-cretaceous-system:
The Cretaceous System is the subject of a geology entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term names a group of layered rocks that sit above the Jurassic rocks. They lie below the oldest Tertiary deposits. In these rocks lie the last records of the great Mesozoic era.

The entry explains that the name comes from white chalk, from the Latin word creta. That chalk was first studied in the basin near Paris and London. Yet the entry stresses that much of the system is not chalk at all. It holds a wide range of rock types. The text then turns to how scholars split and classed these rocks over time.
britannica-1911-cyril-bishop-of-jerusale:
Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem who lived from about three fifteen to three eighty six. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born most likely in Jerusalem, he was ordained a priest in three forty five. He was given charge of teaching new converts in the church there.

Cyril rose to the see of Jerusalem in the year three fifty. His firm hold on the Nicene creed clashed with Arian views near him. He was deposed at times, then restored, then forced out again under Valens. Peace came in three seventy nine when Theodosius let him return home. His chief work is twenty three talks for new converts to baptism.
britannica-1911-emblem:
Emblem, from a Greek word for something put in or inserted, was first used in Greek and Latin for a raised or inlaid ornament. Such ornaments appeared on vases and other vessels. The word also covered mosaic or tessellated work, patterns built up from small set pieces. The entry is only a few lines long and gives the word's first sense before its modern one.

In English the word is confined to a pictured or symbolic showing of some object. It is used above all when the sign serves as a badge or as a heraldic device, a mark worn or borne to stand for a person, a house, or a body. That narrow modern sense is all the entry claims for present use. A reader gets the path of the word in brief, from a thing laid into a surface to a sign that stands for something beyond itself.
britannica-1911-fulk-king-of-jerusalem:
Fulk, king of Jerusalem (born 1092), was son of Fulk IV, count of Anjou. He became count in 1109 and fought Henry I of England as a steady backer of Louis VI of France. In 1127 Henry won him over by betrothing his daughter Matilda to Fulk son Geoffrey Plantagenet. Fulk had already visited the Holy Land in 1120 and befriended the Templars.

In 1128 Baldwin II of Jerusalem, lacking a male heir, offered Fulk his daughter Melisinda in marriage with the succession. They married in 1129, Acre and Tyre forming her dower, and in 1131 Fulk became king. His reign was quiet and prosperous. Beaten by Zengi near Barin in 1137, he later allied with Damascus against the same foe and took Banias in 1140. He strengthened the south with forts such as Blanche Garde. He died in 1143, leaving Baldwin III and Amalric I to follow him.
britannica-1911-gem:
Gem, a word for minerals prized for their shine, hardness, and rarity, is defined in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. In a wide sense it covers stones worn for personal decoration, and it takes in pearl as well. In a narrower sense it means precious stones only after they are cut and polished. Raw stones are called gem-stones instead. At its narrowest, the word means engraved stones such as seals and cameos.

The article treats the subject in two parts. The first part covers the minerals and their general traits. The chief gem-stones named are diamond, ruby, sapphire, emerald, and opal. Lesser stones, such as topaz and tourmaline, are called fancy stones. The second part covers gems in art, meaning engraved work. Man-made stones that copy real ones are left to a separate article.
britannica-1911-mark-system:
Mark System is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a form of social order built on shared land holding. Under this system, small groups of freemen held and farmed land in common. The mark was a self ruling community, both in politics and in daily work. Its first members were likely blood kin.

The entry explains the word first meant a boundary, then the land settlers cleared in the forests of Germany. It describes the mark's land split into forest, meadow, and plough land. Crop rotation ran over two, three, or even six fields. Each member held rights of pasture and a share of the plough land. Affairs were ordered by the markmen meeting in the markmoot.
britannica-1911-mayhem:
Mayhem is an old law term for a maiming attack. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines which wounds counted. The blow had to cost the victim a member used in fight. An arm, a leg, or a front tooth met that test.

Loss of an ear or a back tooth did not count. The hurt had to weaken a man power to defend himself. Earliest English law answered limb for limb in kind. Later practice at common law set fine and prison instead. New statutes in time took aim at maiming and scarring. By 1911 an act of 1861 governed the crime in England. A civil suit could also grow from the same attack. There a judge who saw the wound could raise the sum.
britannica-1911-menahem:
Menahem is a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of a king of Israel in the days of the Old Testament. His name means one who brings comfort in the Hebrew tongue. He seized the throne in a time of turmoil and held it ten years.

The entry recounts harsh acts used to crush a rival revolt in the land. Late in his reign a great Assyrian king marched into the region. Old texts say a huge sum bought that king off from attack. Each rich man in the land was taxed to raise the sum. The unrest he had quelled broke out again soon after his death.
britannica-1911-metric-system:
The metric system is the subject of a measures entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The metre is the base unit of the whole system. In theory the metre is one ten millionth part of a quarter of the earth through Paris. The litre and the gramme are built from that base.

The litre is the volume of a cube with a side one tenth of a metre. The gramme is tied to the weight of water at a set warmth. Calls for measures based on science went back to the seventeen hundreds. The astronomer Jean Picard had proposed a unit based on a pendulum that beat once each second.
britannica-1911-mostaganem:
Mostaganem is the chief town of a district in Oran, Algeria, set on a high flat near the sea coast. The 1911 Britannica entry splits the town in two by a deep gorge with a stream in it. One side holds the European quarter, the other the native quarter, watched by the domes of two holy mens shrines.

A rail line links the town to an inland town handy for old grave tombs. The entry says the town stands on the site of a Roman town, whose port was wrecked by a quake in old times. The port of today is all man made. The town as it stands dates from a Berber age, whose lords built its fort, now a jail, and it passed through many hands in war.
britannica-1911-muscular-system:
Muscular System deals with the flesh parts that move the frame, each part flesh in bulk and cord at the ends. Those cords of white string stuff tie the flesh to the skin of the bones. Where a cord turns past a bone wheel, a small bone can grow in it to cut rub. The knee cap is the case most known.

Each flesh part has blood paths and one or more nerves. The nerve tie counts much for heal work and for form lore. The entry warns that dead tests of pull can mislead. A move is the work of more than one part at once.
britannica-1911-olfactory-system:
Olfactory system is the body gear for the sense of smell. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica walks the nose inside and out. It covers the outer nose that juts from the face. It also covers the twin chambers hidden in the skull.

Bone props the outer nose only at its top. Plates of gristle hold the shape of its lower part. A wall splits the inner nose into two chambers. Thick blood rich lining coats the lower part of that wall. The upper part bears the special smell membrane itself. Curved bones split each side wall into three passages. Air cells open into those passages at set points. The lower chambers serve breath, while the upper ones serve smell.
britannica-1911-roundsman-system:
The roundsman system was a plan of poor relief in old England. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says the parish paid men of property to hire the poor. Pay was set by the parish, not by the work done. It turned on the wants of the man who sought relief. The parish paid back all wages past a fixed sum. A ticket signed by the overseer served as the work pass.

The poor man carried that ticket to the farmer as proof of his right. He brought it back signed as proof the work was done. In some places the parish hired out gangs for a set job. In others the jobless were sold at auction, week by week or month by month. The old and weak fetched less than the strong. The system died with the poor law reform of 1834.
britannica-1911-shechem:
Shechem is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an old town in Palestine, known in modern times as Nablus. It stood south-east of Samaria, between the hills Ebal and Gerizim. The article first meets the town in the book of Genesis, where Jacob and his family settled for a time on land held by the Hivites.

From there the piece follows the town through the Old Testament story. Shechem was set apart as a city of refuge and given to Levites of the tribe of Ephraim. Joshua gave his last speech to the elders there, and the town later stood at the heart of revolts and short-lived kingdoms. The entry ties place, faith, and power together in one short, dense account.
britannica-1911-shem: Shem is treated in a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, drawing on the Bible. The name is the Hebrew word for name, renown, or posterity. In the Bible he is the eldest of the three sons of Noah. The lists of descent in Genesis count Assyrian, Arabian, Aramaean, and Hebrew peoples among his line. From his name the term Semitic was coined as a handy label for these peoples. The entry warns the label is not fully sound, since the Lydians and Elamites sit in the lists too.
britannica-1911-solar-system:
Solar system in astronomy means the sun and all bodies that circle it. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists Earth as one of those circling bodies. The sun holds more than six hundred times the mass of all the rest. That great mass makes it the center of the whole system.

Bodies sort into planets, moons, comets, and meteors in the account. Eight major planets are named, with a belt of minor planets between groups. Inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars in order. Outer planets are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune in order. Moon counts for each planet as then known are given in a table.
britannica-1911-stem:
Stem is a common word with many uses, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica works through them, with botany at the center. In plain speech it names the stalk of a plant or the trunk of a tree. The word also serves for the thin neck of a goblet, a branch of a family, and, in language study, the part of a word that stays fixed.

The entry notes the stem of a ship, the curved piece at the bow where the two sides join. In botany, a stem is an axis that bears leaves, and stem plus leaves make the shoot. It differs from a root in lacking a cap of cells over its growing point, and it tends to climb toward air and light.
britannica-1911-sympathetic-system:
The sympathetic system, in physiology, is a set of nerves and ganglia in the body. It is marked off from the brain and spinal system in form and in work. Men once thought it far more separate from that system than it is. Its ganglia were held to be like the brain and cord in function. That is, they were thought to turn incoming signals into outgoing ones.

New finds show that such work belongs to the brain and cord alone. The ganglia of this system are points where one nerve cell meets others. A signal that arrives by a few cells can be spread to many there. But no true reflex action takes place in those ganglia at all. The system is now known to be a set of conducting paths. Those paths carry signals toward or from the great nerve centres.
britannica-1911-symphonic-poem:
A symphonic poem is a large work for orchestra in one span, and a music entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines the form. The term covers a new style of instrumental music of the past age. That style first showed a clear method in the twelve such works of Liszt. A symphonic poem is not broken into separate movements.

Through all its length and changes of tempo, the work holds together as one. It sets forth a set poetic train of thought, the entry says. That thought must be one that can be put into words, whether it is so put or not. The form of the work is thus set by its programme or poetic idea. Not every piece of programme music earns the name, on that test. The entry sets the symphonic poem apart as a strict form with a poetic core.
britannica-1911-triassic-system:
Triassic System is a geology article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It defines the Triassic as the lowest system of the Mesozoic era, lying above the Permian and below the Jurassic. In the type region of Germany, its chief parts are the Bunter, the Muschelkalk, and the Keuper. A writer named Alberti first grouped them under the name Trias in 1834.

The entry then widens the view beyond Germany. Rich fossil beds found in the Alps and the Mediterranean lands, and later in Asia, changed how geologists read the system. They saw two distinct kinds of Triassic rock building side by side. One was formed on land or in lagoons, and the other was formed in open sea water.
britannica-1911-wem:
Wem is a market town in Shropshire, England, north of Shrewsbury. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes a pleasant town with strong farm trade around it. Its people numbered just under four thousand in 1901. A Norman tower survives in the church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul there.

Flour milling and tanning were its chief trades at that time. Hawkstone, a grand estate, lies in the country nearby. In old times Wem was held as four manors, then as one. Judge Jeffreys later held the lordship and took a baron title from it. A great fire in 1677 caused huge loss across the town.
britannica-1911-winston-salem:
Winston-Salem is the joint name of two neighbouring cities in Forsyth county, North Carolina, and this 1911 Britannica entry treats them together. Winston held 17,167 people in 1910, up from 2,854 in 1880, while Salem held 5,533. Two railways serve both. Since 1899 the post and railway services have used the double name, though the two stay separate municipalities in law.

Winston is the county-seat and a centre of manufacture. Salem is mostly a place of homes and schools, with many old-fashioned houses, though it has factories too. It holds Salem Academy and College, a Moravian school for women opened in 1802, and a normal school for Black students founded in 1892. The country round grows tobacco of very fine quality. The entry credits the tobacco trade, begun in 1872, with the chief share in Winston's growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ad-apostolica:
Ad Apostolicae Dignitatis Apicem is an apostolic letter against Emperor Frederick II. Pope Innocent IV issued it during the Council of Lyons, on 17 July 1245, in the third year of his pontificate. Innocent first sent three legates to Frederick, chief author of the dissensions tearing those parts, showed the way to peace, and promised his own part in restoring it. Frederick agreed to terms, swore to observe them, and at once violated them.

The letter then lists Frederick's crimes. They include perjury, contempt for papal authority by flouting excommunication, and invasion of pontifical territory. They also include broken peace terms with Gregory, oppression of the church in Sicily, and seizure and killing of bishops bound for a council. Suspicion of heresy, conspiracy with Saracens, and unpaid tribute for Sicily, patrimony of St. Peter. For these crimes Innocent declares Frederick unworthy to rule and frees his subjects from obedience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ad-sanctam-be:
Ad Sanctam Beati Petri Sedem is a letter issued by Alexander VII, dated at Rome on 16 October 1656, in the second year of his pontificate. It confirms the decree of Innocent X condemning five points taken from the Augustinus of Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres. Though defined decrees need no backing, Alexander writes because some cast doubt on the definitions or blunt them with false readings, and apostolic authority must promptly remedy the spread of evil.

French bishops had submitted the five points for a clear decision after dispute arose in France. The letter lists them, beginning with claims that some divine precepts are too hard for just men willing to observe them, and that in fallen nature interior grace is not resisted. It declares the points are contained in the Augustinus and condemned in the author's own sense, and it denies that its decision approves other opinions in Jansenius's book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-afflighem:
Afflighem, a Brabant Benedictine abbey near Alost, Belgium, founded by six knights who, abandoning their wild life, resolved to do penance in religion on their former excesses' scene. A church built, they received in 1084 a gift of neighbouring lands from Countess Adela and her sons. The Benedictine rule was adopted, with Wederig as instrument of their conversion, and the abbey later became known for strict observance.

Brabant and Lorraine's dukes and Flanders, Louvain, Brussels, and Bologne's counts patronized and protected it, counting burial in its church a coveted privilege. Several monasteries, Maria-Laach among them, trace their foundation to Afflighem monks. St. Bernard, visiting in 1146, declared he had found angels there, and Our Lady's image is said to have answered his salutation. In 1523 Afflighem joined the Bursfeld Congregation for stricter observance, and in 1569 Mechlin's archbishop became commendatory abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Nidaros, later Trondhjem, owes its Christian beginnings to kings. Norwegians first met the faith on martial expeditions. Haakon the Good, who died in 981, began the work. Converted vikings Olaf Trygvesson, dead in 1002, and Olaf Haraldsson, Saint Olaf, dead in 1030, carried it on, baptized at Andover and Rouen respectively. In 997 Olaf Trygvesson founded Nidaros at the mouth of the River Nid, building a palace and a church there.

From Nidaros he laboured to spread Christianity through Norway, the Orkneys and Shetlands, the Faroes, Iceland, and Greenland. Olaf Haraldsson created an episcopal see at Nidaros and installed the monk Grimkill as bishop. English and German clergy worked beside him. At first Norway's bishops depended on Hamburg-Bremen, then on Lund, primate of Scandinavia. The cathedral stands renewed, though no longer held by the faith that built it. New churches in Saint Olaf's city witness that the Catholic faith lives in Scandinavia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assizes-of-je:
Assizes, in this connection, comes from French asseoir, to seat or place on a seat, hence to put something in its place or determine it. Assise thus came to mean an enactment or statute, and assizes in the plural denotes a court. The Assizes of Jerusalem are the body of laws enacted by Crusaders for the rule of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. They are one collection of legal regulations for tribunals of the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem and of Cyprus.

Parallel codes include the Assizes of Antioch for the Latin principality of Antioch and the Assizes of Romania for the Latin realm of Constantinople. It is wrong, the article warns, to ascribe Jerusalem's assizes to Godfrey de Bouillon merely because he was king of Jerusalem and therefore presumed lawgiver. The entry untangles a famous code from its legendary author and places it among Crusader legal collections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethlehem:
Bethlehem, whose Hebrew name means house of bread, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its Arabic form means house of meat, and some scholars link the name to Lakhmu, a god of Babylonian creation myth, though the entry finds no proof for that guess. Two towns of the name appear in Scripture.

Bethlehem of Judea, five miles south of Jerusalem, outshines its northern namesake, being David's birthplace and, above all, Jesus's. About 10,000 people, almost all Christians, lived there in 1907. Churches, grottoes, and pilgrim sites fill the rest of a place where name, story, and stone meet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-gil-o:
Blessed Gil of Santarem, a Portuguese Dominican, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Vaozela about 1185, son of Coimbra's governor, he died at Santarem in 1265. Boyhood prebends at Braga, Coimbra, Idanha, and Santarem came unasked. But Gil longed not for the Church but for medicine. He studied philosophy and medicine at Coimbra and took a Paris doctorate, working wonderful cures.

A spectre knight twice warned him in his library to change his wicked life. Gil repented, burned his books of magic, and took the Dominican habit at Palencia about 1221. Seven years tormented by a devil's compact ended when the devil surrendered it before Mary's altar. Back in Portugal he became a famed preacher, twice provincial in Spain, and Benedict XIV ratified his cult in 1748.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carem:
Carem was a town of the tribe of Judah. Its name comes from a Hebrew word for vine or vineyard, and it appears in this form only once in the Bible. It occurs only in the Septuagint text of Joshua 15:59, missing with neighboring names from the Vulgate and English versions. Some scholars link it with the Bethacarem of Jeremiah and Esdras, though the link stays open.

Scholars place ancient Carem at 'Ain Karim, a village four miles west of Jerusalem, where village names match the Greek passage. A spring likely took its name from the old town, and the village of about 1,000 people, more than half Muslim, sits on a hill west of the city. A church of the Nativity of John the Baptist stands at its east end. Whether the village is the Baptist's birthplace stays disputed: Fouard doubts it, and Guérin holds to tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-kru:
An entry on Christian Kruik van Adrichem, a Catholic priest and theological writer born at Delft in February 1533. Ordained in 1566, he directed the Convent of Saint Barbara in Delft until the Reformation storm drove him out, and he died at Cologne in June 1585. His works are few but learned, and they made his name among students of the Holy Land.

His Vita Jesu Christi appeared at Antwerp in 1578. His Theatrum Terrae Sanctae et Biblicarum Historiarum at Cologne in 1590 describes Palestine and the antiquities of Jerusalem. It gives a chronology from Adam to the death of John the Apostle in the year 109. The entry rests on Dutch church histories, including Van Heussen and Van Rijn, and a history of Delft of 1729, and it gives the priest his Latin name, Christianus Crucius Adrichomius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elias-of-jeru:
Elias of Jerusalem was a bishop who stood firm for the Council of Chalcedon against Emperor Anastasius I, dying in 518. Anastasius spent most of his reign trying to impose Monophysitism, the teaching that Christ has one nature, on his subjects. At first he sought compromise, but by degrees he went over wholly to the Monophysites, deposing Macedonius of Constantinople in 511 and backing a fierce persecution under Timothy I.

With Flavian of Antioch, Elias was one of only two Catholic bishops who resisted the imperial drive to scrap Chalcedon. When the government called a synod at Sidon in 512 to condemn the council, it was chiefly Elias who blocked that result. An Arab by birth, schooled in an Egyptian monastery and driven out by a Monophysite patriarch in 457, he had come to Palestine and risen to the see of Jerusalem. The entry is a portrait of stubborn orthodoxy under an emperor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haarlem:
Holland's Diocese of Haarlem was carved from the sprawling medieval see of Utrecht by Paul IV in 1559, with its cathedral at St. Bavo's and the Abbey of Egmond as its revenue. Its first bishop, Nicolas van Nieuwland, held a synod in 1564 and pleaded with the Duke of Alva for leniency, but gout and slowness forced his resignation in 1569.

Godfried van Mierlo, his successor, reconsecrated the pillaged cathedral in 1573.
